title: Voyager 1 Is About to Be One Light-Day From Earth — and You Can Wave Back
excerpt: On Wednesday, November 18, at 5:16 a.m. Eastern, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object ever to reach one light-day from Earth — 16 billion miles away.
content:
On Wednesday morning, November 18, a spacecraft launched before most of today's college students were born will cross a line no human-made object has ever reached. At 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern time, Voyager 1 will be one light-day from Earth — the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 16.09 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers).

Voyager 1 launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on September 5, 1977, to study the outer planets. It flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, then kept going — out of the planets, out of the Sun's protective bubble, and into interstellar space, which it entered in 2012. When it crosses the one-light-day mark on November 18, the spacecraft will have taken 49 years, two months and 11 days to get there.

Nothing will change on the spacecraft when it crosses the line. The milestone is symbolic — a way to grasp a distance so large that everyday units fail. Light, moving at about 186,000 miles every second, takes a full day to make the trip. A radio command sent from Earth now takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and another full day for the reply to come back — a 48-hour round trip for every exchange.

Still flying on 1970s hardware

The spacecraft is still working. Of its original ten science instruments, two remain switched on: the magnetometer and the plasma wave instrument, still sending back data from interstellar space. Its transmitter puts out about 23 watts — roughly the power of a refrigerator bulb — yet NASA's Deep Space Network still hears it across 16 billion miles, at about 160 bits per second.

Voyager 1 is headed toward a faint star more than 17 light-years away called Gliese 445. It is expected to pass within about 1.7 light-years of that star — in 40,000 years. Its twin, Voyager 2, took a different path to visit Uranus and Neptune, and is on pace to reach one light-day from Earth in November 2035, nine years from now.

How Laredo can join in

NASA is marking the moment with a public event called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." After sunset on Tuesday, November 17, people around the world are invited to flash Voyager's call sign — V-G-R — in Morse code toward the sky, using phones, flashlights, or even whole buildings. NASA has an automated flasher on its website that does the Morse code for you.

On Wednesday, November 19, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will host a moderated discussion about the mission, available through NASA Live.

For readers here in Webb County, the invitation is the same as everywhere else on the planet: step outside Tuesday night, point a light at the sky, and wave back at the farthest thing humanity has ever built.
